title: The lac Operon: How Bacteria Regulate Genes

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What did Monod call the pattern in which E. coli given glucose and lactose grows on glucose first, pauses, then grows on lactose?
cards.back: Diauxie, two-step growth.
cards.why: During the pause the cells make the lactose-handling proteins in quantity.
cards.quote: saw that E. coli given glucose and lactose uses the glucose first, pauses, then grows on lactose.

cards.front: In wild-type E. coli, what two conditions give high lac operon expression?
cards.back: Lactose present and glucose scarce.
cards.why: Lactose releases the repressor; scarce glucose lets CAP with cAMP help the promoter.
cards.quote: In wild-type E. coli, high lac expression requires lactose and scarce glucose.

cards.front: A set of genes transcribed together under one control is an {{c1::operon}}.
cards.quote: A set of genes transcribed together under one control is an operon.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: In the E. coli lac operon, what do lacZ and lacY encode?
cards.back: lacZ encodes β-galactosidase, which splits lactose into glucose and galactose. lacY encodes the permease that carries lactose in.
cards.quote: lacZ encodes β-galactosidase, which splits lactose into glucose and galactose. lacY encodes the permease that carries lactose in.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: How can the three lac genes be controlled together yet give three separate proteins?
cards.back: One promoter makes one polycistronic mRNA, which is read into three separate proteins.
cards.quote: All three are transcribed from one promoter into one polycistronic mRNA (an mRNA carrying several genes), read into three separate proteins.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: What does the lac repressor bind, and why is this called negative control?
cards.back: It binds the operator and keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing the genes. The regulator stops expression, so control is negative.
cards.quote: The repressor binds the operator, a short DNA site at the start of transcription, and keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing the genes
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: What is the natural inducer of the lac operon, and is it lactose itself?
cards.back: Allolactose, which β-galactosidase makes from a little incoming lactose. Lactose itself is not the inducer.
cards.quote: The natural inducer is allolactose, which β-galactosidase makes from a little incoming lactose by joining the same sugars with a different bond; lactose itself is not the inducer.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: How does the inducer free the operator in the lac system?
cards.back: It binds the repressor at a separate site, changes its shape (allostery), and lowers its affinity for the operator.
cards.quote: It binds the repressor and changes its shape, lowering its affinity for the operator.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: Why do geneticists often use IPTG instead of lactose to induce the lac operon?
cards.back: IPTG binds the repressor but is not broken down by β-galactosidase, so the cell does not use it up. Such an inducer is gratuitous.
cards.quote: IPTG, a synthetic compound that binds the repressor but is not broken down by β-galactosidase, so the cell does not use it up.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: Lactose entry needs the permease and its use needs β-galactosidase, yet both are made by the operon lactose switches on. How can an uninduced cell start?
cards.back: Repression leaks, so an uninduced cell holds a few copies of each protein.
cards.quote: repression leaks, so an uninduced cell can hold a few copies of each protein.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: What does CAP with cAMP bound do at the lac promoter, and is this positive or negative control?
cards.back: It binds just upstream of the promoter and contacts RNA polymerase's α subunit, helping polymerase bind and start. Positive control.
cards.quote: CAP with cyclic AMP bound attaches just upstream of the promoter and contacts the C-terminal part of RNA polymerase's α subunit, helping polymerase bind and start
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: What is inducer exclusion in E. coli, and how does it lower lac expression?
cards.back: While glucose is taken up, a transport-system protein blocks the lac permease. Less lactose enters, less allolactose forms, and more repressor stays on the operator.
cards.quote: This inducer exclusion is a major glucose effect in E. coli: less lactose enters, less allolactose forms, and more repressor remains on the operator.
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: Wild-type E. coli has no lactose and no glucose. Is lac transcription high?
cards.back: No, it is very low. The repressor stays on the operator, and CAP cannot overcome a bound repressor.
cards.quote: CAP cannot overcome a bound repressor
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: Wild-type E. coli has both lactose and glucose. Lac expression is lower than with lactose alone. Give the two causes.
cards.back: Less active CAP (cAMP is lower when glucose is plentiful, in the classic account) and inducer exclusion, which limits lactose entry.
cards.why: How much the cAMP change matters in living cells is debated.
cards.quote: In the classic account, cAMP is higher when glucose is scarce and lower when glucose is plentiful; how much this change matters in living cells is debated.
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: A mutation in the CAP-binding site stops CAP–cAMP from attaching. With lactose present and glucose absent, does lac expression match the wild-type high level?
cards.back: No. Allolactose still releases the repressor, but the weak promoter has lost CAP's help, so expression stays well below the wild-type induced level.
cards.quote: Allolactose can release the repressor, but the weak promoter has lost CAP's help, so expression remains well below the wild-type induced level.
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: A lac mutant that makes β-galactosidase with or without inducer is {{c1::constitutive}}.
cards.quote: Some mutants made β-galactosidase with or without inducer; they are constitutive.
cards.section: The partial diploid: telling a site from a product

cards.front: In a haploid cell, why can a constitutive I⁻ mutant not be told apart from a constitutive Oᶜ mutant, and what fixes this?
cards.back: Both give enzyme without inducer. A second copy of the lac region in the same cell (a partial diploid) lets the two be compared.
cards.quote: In a haploid cell, the two look the same. How can a broken repressor gene be distinguished from a broken binding site?
cards.section: The partial diploid: telling a site from a product

cards.front: A cell with chromosomal lac plus F′ lac is a partial diploid, or {{c1::merodiploid}}: diploid only for those genes.
cards.quote: A cell with chromosomal lac plus F′ lac is a partial diploid, or merodiploid: diploid only for those genes.
cards.section: The partial diploid: telling a site from a product

cards.front: In cis–trans logic, which lac elements act in cis and which can act in trans?
cards.back: DNA sites such as the operator act in cis. Diffusible products such as the repressor can act in trans.
cards.quote: DNA sites act in cis; diffusible regulators can act in trans.
cards.section: The partial diploid: telling a site from a product

cards.front: In a cell without glucose, genotype I⁻ Z⁺ / F′ I⁺ Z⁻ (chromosome / F′). What is β-galactosidase activity without and with IPTG?
cards.back: Basal without IPTG, induced with IPTG. The only Z⁺ sits beside a normal chromosomal operator, and F′ repressor diffuses to it. I⁻ is recessive.
cards.quote: The only Z⁺ is beside a normal chromosomal operator, and F′ repressor diffuses to it.
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: In a cell without glucose, genotype Oᶜ Z⁺ / F′ O⁺ Z⁻ (chromosome / F′, both I⁺). What is β-galactosidase activity without and with IPTG?
cards.back: Constitutive in both. The working Z⁺ is linked in cis to Oᶜ, which binds no repressor.
cards.quote: The working Z⁺ is linked in cis to Oᶜ.
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: In a cell without glucose, genotype Oᶜ Z⁻ / F′ O⁺ Z⁺ (chromosome / F′, both I⁺). Is the enzyme constitutive or inducible?
cards.back: Inducible. The Oᶜ copy is transcribed all the time, but its Z⁻ makes nothing active, and the working Z⁺ sits beside O⁺.
cards.why: Same two mutations as the Oᶜ Z⁺ / F′ O⁺ Z⁻ case, swapped between copies, change the answer: a cis-acting site.
cards.quote: The Oᶜ copy is transcribed all the time, but its Z⁻ makes nothing active.
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: What phenotype should Iˢ Z⁻ / F′ I⁺ Z⁺ show without and with IPTG?
cards.back: Uninducible. Iˢ repressor binds the operator beside F′ Z⁺ and stays bound with IPTG. Iˢ is dominant to I⁺.
cards.quote: The Iˢ protein diffuses to the normal operator beside F′ Z⁺ and remains bound when IPTG is added.
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: Why can an I⁻ᵈ mutation be dominant even though a plain I⁻ is recessive?
cards.back: I⁻ᵈ subunits assemble with normal subunits but bind DNA poorly, so mixed repressor binds the operator poorly (dominant-negative).
cards.quote: make subunits that assemble with normal subunits but bind DNA poorly or not at all
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: In I⁻ᵈ Z⁻ / F′ I⁺ O⁺ Z⁺, does putting the working reporter on the F′ protect it from I⁻ᵈ?
cards.back: No. The defective subunits are products that act in trans and can mix with normal subunits, impairing repression at the F′ operator.
cards.quote: The defective subunits are products that act in trans.
cards.section: Worked problem: read the reporter first

cards.front: A haploid E. coli with a non-functional repressor (I⁻) is grown with no lactose, no IPTG and no glucose. Is β-galactosidase activity low or high?
cards.back: High. With no working repressor nothing blocks the operator, and with glucose absent CAP–cAMP is available.
cards.why: Rests on negative control: the repressor, when working, is what stops expression.
cards.quote: and keeps RNA polymerase from transcribing the genes: negative control, where the regulator stops expression.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: A lac reporter strain makes 1500 units of β-galactosidase with inducer and 30 units without. What is the repression factor?
cards.back: Repression factor = activity with inducer ÷ activity without inducer = 1500 ÷ 30 = 50.
cards.quote: repression factor = enzyme activity with inducer ÷ enzyme activity without inducer
cards.section: Auxiliary operators and repression factor

cards.front: A wild-type-CAP E. coli strain carries Oᶜ and is grown with both lactose and glucose. Compared with growth on lactose alone, would you expect lac expression to stay as high, and why?
cards.back: Possibly lower. Oᶜ removes the repressor effect, but in the classic account glucose could still reduce active CAP–cAMP, though how much that matters in living cells is debated.
cards.why: Rests on: high expression needs CAP–cAMP, and glucose lowers cAMP.
cards.quote: In the classic account, cAMP is higher when glucose is scarce and lower when glucose is plentiful; how much this change matters in living cells is debated.
cards.section: CAP and cAMP: the glucose-sensitive input

cards.front: You isolate a new constitutive lac mutant, m. Design partial diploids that tell whether it is a recessive I⁻, a dominant-negative I⁻ᵈ, or an operator Oᶜ.
cards.back: First test m Z⁺ / F′ I⁺ O⁺ Z⁻. If it becomes inducible, m is a recessive I⁻. If still constitutive, m is I⁻ᵈ or Oᶜ. Then test m Z⁻ / F′ I⁺ O⁺ Z⁺: inducible means Oᶜ, constitutive means I⁻ᵈ.
cards.why: Move the reporter and ask whether the effect moves with it.
cards.quote: The logic: move the reporter and ask whether the effect moves with it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A constitutive mutation m gives these results, grown without glucose. In m Z⁺ / F′ I⁺ O⁺ Z⁻ the enzyme is made with and without IPTG. In m Z⁻ / F′ I⁺ O⁺ Z⁺ it is made only with IPTG. Is m I⁻, I⁻ᵈ or Oᶜ?
cards.back: Oᶜ. The first result rules out recessive I⁻, and the second rules out I⁻ᵈ, which would act in trans. Only a cis-acting site fits.
cards.quote: If m is Oᶜ, expression is inducible: the Oᶜ copy's Z⁻ makes nothing active, and the F′ Z⁺ sits beside a normal operator.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: I⁺ Z⁺ donor genes enter I⁻ Z⁻ recipients with no inducer, and donor enzyme synthesis is blocked. β-Galactosidase appears, rises, then stops rising, and IPTG restores synthesis. What does this suggest about the I⁺ product?
cards.back: It is a diffusible product that builds up after entry and then represses. IPTG releases it, so Z⁺ was still present.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that diffusible regulators act in trans.
cards.quote: DNA sites act in cis; diffusible regulators can act in trans.
cards.section: The partial diploid: telling a site from a product

cards.front: How can one lac repressor tetramer repress with more than one operator?
cards.back: It can hold two operators at once, looping the DNA between them. The lac region has three operators, O1, O2 and O3.
cards.quote: One tetramer can hold two operators at once, looping the DNA between them.
cards.section: The switch: a repressor that lets go

cards.front: How does the trp repressor differ from the lac repressor in what it needs to bind the operator?
cards.back: Trp repressor alone binds the operator poorly; tryptophan binds it and enables binding, so the end product shuts down the pathway. The trp operon is repressible, the lac operon inducible.
cards.quote: The trp repressor alone binds the operator poorly; tryptophan binds it and enables operator binding, so the end product shuts down its pathway.
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: What is the attenuator in the E. coli trp operon?
cards.back: A site in the leader, before the first structural gene, where transcription can stop after it has started.
cards.quote: Transcription can stop in a leader before the first structural gene, at the attenuator.
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: Why can trp attenuation work in bacteria but not in a eukaryotic nucleus?
cards.back: A bacterial ribosome translates the leader while RNA polymerase transcribes just ahead. In a eukaryotic nucleus transcription and translation are separated.
cards.quote: Bacteria have no nucleus, so a ribosome translates the leader while RNA polymerase transcribes just ahead
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: When tryptophan is plentiful, what happens at the trp leader?
cards.back: The ribosome moves past the two Trp codons and covers region 2. Regions 3 and 4 pair, forming the terminator, and polymerase stops.
cards.quote: With region 2 covered, regions 3 and 4 pair, the terminator forms, and polymerase stops.
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: When tryptophan is scarce, what happens at the trp leader?
cards.back: The ribosome stalls at the Trp codons, short of region 2. Region 2 pairs with region 3, so no terminator forms and polymerase continues into the structural genes.
cards.quote: Region 2 pairs with region 3, the terminator cannot form, and polymerase continues into the structural genes.
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: The two Trp codons in the trp leader are replaced with codons for another amino acid. Cells are starved of tryptophan only. Does readthrough rise?
cards.back: No. The ribosome does not stall at the replacement codons. It covers region 2, the 3:4 terminator forms, and readthrough stays low.
cards.quote: It covers region 2, allowing the 3:4 terminator to form, so readthrough stays low.
cards.section: The trp operon: a repressor that needs a partner, and a brake on the ribosome

cards.front: In a test tube with no ribosomes, only about 5 percent of transcripts read through the E. coli trp attenuator. What does this suggest about the ribosome's role?
cards.back: Only about 5 percent read through with no ribosomes, so in the cell model most readthrough needs a translating ribosome to keep 3:4 from pairing.
cards.why: Rests on the 3:4 hairpin being a terminator and 2:3 pairing blocking it.
cards.quote: only about 5 percent of transcripts read through the E. coli trp attenuator
cards.section: Attenuation in a test tube
